lesson.title: One Set or Two: Haploid and Diploid Cells
lesson.summary: Diploid cells carry two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, while haploid cells carry only one set, a distinction that makes sexual reproduction possible without doubling chromosome number each generation.
lesson.body:
Eukaryotic cells package their DNA into structures called chromosomes, and the number of chromosomes a cell carries falls into one of two basic categories. A diploid cell carries two complete sets of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent. A haploid cell carries only a single complete set. This distinction, abbreviated 2n for diploid and n for haploid, where n is the number of chromosomes in one full set, turns out to be essential for how sexual reproduction works.

In humans, nearly all the cells that make up the body, called somatic cells, are diploid, carrying 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs. Each pair consists of one chromosome from your mother and one from your father. The two members of a homologous pair are not identical to each other, but they carry genes for the same traits at the same locations, or loci, along the chromosome, sometimes with different versions of a gene, called alleles, at a given locus. This is different from sister chromatids, which appear later during the cell cycle: sister chromatids are the two exact copies of a single chromosome produced when that chromosome is replicated during S phase, and they are genetically identical to each other, unlike the two members of a homologous pair.

Human gametes, sperm and eggs, are the major example of haploid cells in the body: each carries just 23 chromosomes, one member from each homologous pair, with no matching partner alongside it. This halving is not arbitrary. When a haploid sperm fertilizes a haploid egg, their chromosomes combine to restore the full diploid number of 46 in the resulting zygote, with the normal pairing of maternal and paternal chromosomes reestablished. Without some mechanism to first cut the chromosome number in half before fertilization, chromosome number would double with every generation, which is obviously not what happens.

That halving mechanism is meiosis, a specialized version of the cell cycle explored in the next chapter, which uses the same basic replication machinery covered in the general cell cycle, including a normal S phase, but follows it with a division process that produces haploid rather than diploid daughter cells. Understanding the difference between diploid and haploid, and between homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids, is the foundation for everything meiosis does.
